22.title: Marcus doesn't want to get up
22.hook: the emperor argues with himself under the blankets: was I made to lie here warm?
22.carry: up, to do a human's work
22.howItsDone: Many people who practice Stoicism today begin the morning with a short reflection, often reading Marcus Aurelius, and remind themselves of the day's duties and the kind of person they want to be in them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Rumi, and a field beyond our ideas of doing wrong and doing right, where he'll meet you. That closed camp one: twenty-one words.

A cold tent, maybe somewhere near the Danube, in the second century. It's early. The most powerful man in the world is lying under his blankets, and he does not want to get up. He's Marcus Aurelius, emperor of Rome. And instead of getting up, or staying put, he does something odd. He argues with himself about it, in writing.
screen: `A COLD TENT BY THE DANUBE.` → `THE EMPEROR STAYS IN BED.` → `HE ARGUES, IN WRITING.`

segments.voice: Welcome to camp two, the stories: from today, the words become people. Marcus was a Stoic. The Stoics were philosophers of ancient Greece and Rome who taught that a good life is built from what you do with what happens to you. He kept a private notebook, the one from camp one, and much of it was probably written on military campaigns in his last decade. Book five opens right there, under the blankets. In George Long's translation, he tells himself that when he rises unwillingly, he should remember: "I am rising to the work of a human being." Then he asks: "Or have I been made for this, to lie in the bed-clothes and keep myself warm?" And he answers himself back: but it's more pleasant here. The emperor of Rome, haggling with his own pillow. So he looks outside. The little plants, the birds, the ants, the spiders, the bees, all busy doing their part to keep the world in order. And you, a human being, won't do yours? It's easy to hear that as a scolding. But notice what he doesn't say. Not get up to be rich, or famous, or because the empire needs you. Get up because there's a human's work to do, and you're a human. Being kind, being fair, being useful to the people around you: for a Stoic, that was the job description. The alarm isn't a punishment. It's a reminder of what you're for. And this isn't a sage who never struggled. It's a tired man winning a very small argument, one morning at a time, and writing it down so he'd remember.

Ask Marcus's question, what's the human's work waiting for me today, and let one answer come: a person to be kind to, or a job to do well.
Marcus Aurelius. An emperor arguing with his own blankets, and reminding himself what a human being is for.

23.title: The master and the leg
23.hook: enslaved, Epictetus warns his master he'll break his leg, it breaks, and he says calmly "didn't I tell you?"
23.howItsDone: Stoic practice sorts troubles into what is in our power and what is not, and puts effort only into the first: our own judgments, choices and responses.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Marcus Aurelius, the emperor haggling with his blankets, and getting up to do a human's work.
screen: `MARCUS AURELIUS — UP, TO DO A HUMAN'S WORK.`

segments.voice: Picture this. A wealthy man in Rome, so the story goes, starts twisting the leg of Epictetus, the man he owns. Hard. For no reason we're told. And Epictetus, instead of crying out, looks at his master and speaks, quietly: you're going to break it.
screen: `A WEALTHY MAN IN ROME.` → `THE MASTER TWISTS HIS LEG.` → `YOU'RE GOING TO BREAK IT.`

segments.voice: He was born enslaved, at the very bottom of the empire, in a town in what's now Turkey. Epictetus, the only name we have for him, is a Greek word for acquired. Bought. His owner was himself a former slave of the emperor Nero's household. The master keeps twisting. The leg breaks. And Epictetus says, calmly: didn't I tell you it would break? No scream, no curse. Now, honesty about the source. This story isn't from Epictetus. It comes from an ancient writer named Celsus, in a book attacking Christianity, and we only have it because a Christian scholar, Origen, quoted Celsus in order to answer him. Another ancient source says his lameness came from illness, not cruelty. So we can't be sure it happened. But we know Epictetus was lame, and we know what he taught about it. In George Long's translation of his handbook: "Lameness is an impediment to the leg, but not to the will." And the handbook's first line: "Of things some are in our power, and others are not." A twisted leg isn't in your power, if someone stronger is doing the twisting. What you say while it happens may still be yours. What this doesn't mean: that cruelty is fine, or that pain doesn't hurt, or that someone being harmed should just keep quiet. If it happened, it was wrong. The story is about something smaller and stranger: even at the very bottom, with no power at all, a person can still choose the voice they answer in. Epictetus spent the rest of his life teaching that.
screen: `HIS NAME MEANS ACQUIRED.` · `A STORY TOLD BY A CRITIC.` · `IMPEDIMENT TO THE LEG, NOT THE WILL.` · `CRUELTY IS STILL WRONG.` · then, large: `THE VOICE YOU ANSWER IN.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath settle, then gently notice one pain you can't change today: a sore back, a diagnosis, a person who won't change, a loss. Don't push it away and don't feed it; breathe beside it, and ask quietly what part of it is yours, maybe only the voice you answer in. If it's too much today, just come back to the breath.
Epictetus. An enslaved man, a broken leg, and a calm answer: didn't I tell you?
Your line: said calmly. Even with no power at all, the voice you answer in can stay yours. That's day twenty-three.

24.title: Epictetus goes free
24.hook: freed, he teaches in Rome, is banished with all philosophers by Domitian, and opens a school at Nicopolis around 93 CE
24.howItsDone: Modern Stoics often keep a short written list of what is truly in their power, their own choices and responses, and read the Discourses and Handbook of Epictetus as a daily guide.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Epictetus, enslaved and lamed, and the voice he answered in: said calmly.

Picture it: a lame, formerly enslaved man is teaching the sons of the powerful in Rome how to live. Then the emperor Domitian decides philosophers are a nuisance, and throws them all out of the city. So where does a lame teacher with no city go now?
screen: `A LAME MAN TEACHING IN ROME.` → `PHILOSOPHERS ARE A NUISANCE.` → `THE EMPEROR THROWS THEM OUT.`

segments.voice: At some point, and we don't know exactly when or how, Epictetus was set free. He'd already been studying philosophy while enslaved, with a Roman Stoic teacher named Musonius Rufus. Now he taught it himself. Then came the exile; historians still debate the exact year. He lost his city, his students, whatever he'd built. So he went across the sea to Nicopolis, a town on the western coast of Greece, and opened a school. And people came. Young men traveled, some of them a long way, to sit on hard benches and be questioned by this lame teacher. As far as we know, he never wrote a book. We have his teaching only because one student, Arrian, wrote down what he said, and later published it as the Discourses and a short handbook. Through them, you can hear him in class. He imagines a tyrant threatening him. You'll chain me? You can chain my leg. But my will, not even Zeus himself can take that. A thief once stole the iron lamp from his little shrine at home. His response: next time I'll buy a clay one. Then the twist: the thief lost more than I did. He paid for a lamp by becoming a thief. The Greek word he kept coming back to was prohairesis, usually translated will, or choice: your power to decide how you'll meet what happens. Owned, lamed, freed, exiled: everything outside kept being taken. The school at Nicopolis was real, with benches and walls. But the school he actually taught was one you carry inside, and no emperor can banish it.
screen: `SET FREE, SOMEHOW.` · `A SCHOOL AT NICOPOLIS.` · `YOU CAN CHAIN MY LEG.` · `THE THIEF LOST MORE.` · then, large: `THE SCHOOL IS INSIDE.`

Prohairesis. Will, or choice: the part of you that decides how to meet what happens, and the one thing Epictetus never lost.
Your line: the school is inside. Benches and walls can be taken; that one can't. See you tomorrow.

25.title: Zeno's shipwreck
25.hook: a merchant loses his cargo of purple dye off Athens and wanders into a bookshop
25.carry: I sailed well when I was wrecked
25.howItsDone: Stoics practice looking at a setback as material to work with rather than simply a disaster, asking what response is still in their power after the loss.

segments.voice: Yesterday: prohairesis, the will no emperor could banish, and a school you carry inside. Today, back to where the Stoics began.

A merchant ship, carrying a cargo of purple dye from Phoenicia, goes down somewhere off the coast near Athens. The cargo, the fortune, gone into the sea. The merchant makes it to shore with, as far as we know, nothing. His name is Zeno, from Citium, a city on the island of Cyprus. Centuries before the emperor and the enslaved teacher, he's the man who started it all.
screen: `A CARGO OF PURPLE DYE.` → `THE SHIP GOES DOWN.` → `THE MAN WHO STARTED IT ALL.`

segments.voice: Our source is Diogenes Laërtius, who wrote lives of the Greek philosophers centuries after Zeno, collecting stories from older books, some already disagreeing. So this is the story the ancient world told about Zeno, not a court record. Shipwrecked, broke, around thirty years old, Zeno walks up from the harbor into Athens. He doesn't know anyone. He wanders into a bookseller's shop and sits down. The bookseller is reading aloud, or Zeno picks up, a book about Socrates, written by one of Socrates's students. Zeno is hooked. The way Socrates lived, questioning everything, owning almost nothing, unafraid, hits him right in the chest. He's lost everything he owned, and on the same trip he finds what he'll spend the rest of his life on. Years later, Diogenes says, Zeno looked back on the wreck and said something like: I made a good voyage when I was shipwrecked. Another version has him thanking Fortune for driving him to philosophy. Either way, the man who lost a fortune at sea founded a school that would reach an emperor in his tent, an enslaved teacher in Nicopolis, and people reading the Stoics on their phones today. Now, gently. Not every loss sends you somewhere good, and nobody should tell a grieving person that everything happens for a reason. The Stoics didn't say the wreck was good. They said what you do after the wreck is still yours. Zeno's cargo sank. Zeno walked into a bookshop.
screen: `A STORY TOLD CENTURIES LATER.` · `BROKE, IN A BOOKSHOP.` · `A BOOK ABOUT SOCRATES.` · `NOT EVERY LOSS IS A GIFT.` · then, large: `I SAILED WELL WHEN I WAS WRECKED.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath settle, then look back for one loss that, in the end, sent you somewhere good: a job that ended, a plan that fell through, a move you didn't want. Not the worst loss, just one where you can see the bookshop now: what sank, and where you washed up. If none comes, that's all right; rest in the breath.

26.title: Follow that man
26.hook: Zeno asks the bookseller where men like Socrates can be found, and Crates the Cynic walks past
26.carry: nothing terrible has happened to you
26.howItsDone: In the ancient schools, people learned philosophy by attaching themselves to a living teacher and following them about; many people today still seek out a teacher or a community to learn from in person.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Zeno's shipwreck. A fortune lost at sea, and a merchant hooked on a book about Socrates in a bookshop.
screen: `ZENO'S SHIPWRECK — I SAILED WELL WHEN I WAS WRECKED.`

segments.voice: Zeno looks up from the page. Socrates has been dead for generations, so he asks the bookseller: where can I find men like this? Real ones. Alive. And right then, as if the story had been waiting for its cue, a strange figure walks past the shop door. The bookseller points at him and says three words. Follow that man.
screen: `ZENO LOOKS UP FROM THE PAGE.` → `WHERE CAN I FIND MEN LIKE THIS?` → `A STRANGE FIGURE WALKS PAST.`

segments.voice: The man walking past was Crates, a Cynic philosopher. The Cynics were the punk rockers of ancient Greece. They owned almost nothing, slept in public, said exactly what they thought, and mocked anything fake. The name comes from the Greek for dog-like, because they lived as openly as dogs. Crates had been born rich, in Thebes, and given his wealth away. Ancient writers say people called him the door-opener, because he walked into any house he liked and gave the family advice, and they were glad to see him. A woman named Hipparchia, from a wealthy family, fell in love with him, chose his life of the road over her comfortable one, and became a philosopher in her own right. So Zeno followed, and became Crates's student. But Zeno was shy, and the Cynics were shameless on purpose. Diogenes Laërtius tells this story. Crates hands Zeno a pot of lentil soup and tells him to carry it through a busy part of Athens. Zeno, embarrassed, tries to hide it under his cloak. Crates cracks the pot with his staff. Soup runs down Zeno's legs. Zeno runs. And Crates calls after him, roughly: why are you running, my little Phoenician? Nothing terrible has happened to you. Embarrassment, Crates was saying, isn't harm. And look at how it all began. A curious question, asked out loud. A stranger walking past. And the nerve to get up from a bookseller's bench and follow him out the door.
screen: `THE CYNICS: DOG-LIKE, AND PROUD.` · `CRATES, THE DOOR-OPENER.` · `A POT OF LENTIL SOUP.` · `EMBARRASSMENT ISN'T HARM.` · then, large: `FOLLOW THAT MAN.`

27.title: The painted porch
27.hook: Zeno teaches in a public colonnade, and the school takes its name from the porch
27.howItsDone: Stoicism has always been practiced in ordinary life rather than apart from it: its followers aim to be steady and just in public roles, at work and in the family.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Crates, the Cynic who cracked a pot of soup and told a shy Zeno that embarrassment isn't harm.
screen: `CRATES — NOTHING TERRIBLE HAS HAPPENED TO YOU.`

segments.voice: Where do you teach, when you have no money, no building, no school? Around the year three hundred BCE, after years learning from Crates and other teachers in Athens, that was Zeno's problem. He picked the middle of the city. Not behind a wall, not in a private garden. On the edge of the marketplace, the agora, where everyone walked past all day long.
screen: `NO MONEY, NO BUILDING.` → `THE MIDDLE OF THE CITY.` → `THE EDGE OF THE MARKET.`

segments.voice: He taught under a stoa: a colonnade, a long roof held up by a row of columns, open on one side, where people could get out of the sun or the rain. Athens had several. Zeno's was the Stoa Poikile, the painted porch, because its walls held great paintings by famous artists, including a scene of the Battle of Marathon, the day Athens fought off a Persian invasion. Picture it. Merchants shouting in the market. People sheltering from the heat. Travelers staring at the paintings. And a thin, serious man from Cyprus walking up and down between the columns, talking, while anyone who wanted to could stop and listen. Diogenes Laërtius says his followers were first called Zenonians, after him. But the name that stuck was the place: people who met at the porch. The Stoics. Other schools in Athens met in other kinds of places. Plato's Academy was in a grove outside the city walls. Epicurus gathered his friends in a private garden. Each place suited its school, and the Stoics' fit is almost too good. Their whole teaching was about living well in the middle of ordinary life: the market, the law court, the family, the army. Not by escaping the world, but in it. Two thousand three hundred years later, the name of a building is still the name of a way of life. Every time someone says stoic, they're pointing, without knowing it, at a painted porch in the middle of a crowd.
screen: `A LONG ROOF ON A ROW OF COLUMNS.` · `PAINTINGS OF MARATHON.` · `ZENONIANS, THEN STOICS.` · `LIVING WELL IN THE MIDDLE OF LIFE.` · then, large: `WISDOM IN THE OPEN.`

segments.voice: Wherever you are, a bus, a cafe, a park, or at home picturing a busy street you know, sit with your eyes open or half closed. Let the noise and the movement go on around you, people passing, sounds coming and going; you don't have to escape it to be steady. Breathe in the middle of it, the way Zeno taught in the middle of the market.
Stoa. A porch with columns, open to the street, and the place that gave the Stoics their name.
Your line: wisdom in the open. Not behind a wall, but in the middle of the crowd. See you at the wells tomorrow.

28.title: Cleanthes carries water
28.hook: the boxer who drew water at night so he could study by day
28.howItsDone: Stoics treat ordinary tasks as a place to practice virtue, doing humble work carefully and without resentment; Cleanthes's life is still told as the example.

segments.voice: Yesterday: stoa, the painted porch on the edge of the market that gave a school its name, and wisdom in the open.

Every night, while Athens sleeps, a big man with a boxer's shoulders hauls water up from the wells in the gardens around the city, bucket after bucket, so the plants will live. Every morning, tired, hands raw, he walks to the painted porch and sits down to listen to Zeno. His name is Cleanthes. He came to Athens, the story goes, with almost no money in his pocket. He wanted to study philosophy all day. But he had to eat.
screen: `WATER AT NIGHT, WISDOM BY DAY.` → `A BOXER AT THE PAINTED PORCH.` → `NO MONEY IN HIS POCKET.`

segments.voice: Diogenes Laërtius tells the rest. People noticed this strong young man who studied all day and never seemed to work. How was he living? He was summoned before the city's council to explain himself. Cleanthes brought witnesses: the gardener whose water he drew, and a woman whose grain he ground. The council was so impressed they voted him a gift of money. And Zeno, his teacher, told him not to take it. The Athenians started calling him the well-drawer. He was, the story says, a slow learner, and other students called him the donkey. His reply: fine, then I'm the only one strong enough to carry Zeno's load. He couldn't afford writing material, so he wrote his notes on oyster shells and the flat shoulder bones of oxen. And the ending: when Zeno died, the man who took over the school wasn't the quickest student. It was Cleanthes. The water carrier. The lesson people have drawn from his life is simple: no task is beneath a person who does it well. The humble work and the high work are the same work, done by the same character. And that's week four. Marcus Aurelius. Epictetus. Prohairesis. Zeno's shipwreck. Follow that man. Stoa. And Cleanthes, carrying water. An emperor, an enslaved man, a shipwrecked merchant, a Cynic, and a boxer with a bucket. The Stoics woke up.
